movePayload.answer: Created Strategic Move 8788086c-ab4a-4091-a377-dbe345a43ddc: Commerce Cloud Sequencing and CDP Scope Reset.

turns.user: Our ecom mix is 18.5% versus a peer median of 24%. We have three active investments that all touch this gap: Commerce Cloud Optimization (the replatform), the Einstein activation we paid for but never turned on, and the CDP Migration Phase 2 that is over-scoped. We also have the SAP ERP Future Decision pending which affects our data foundation. The board is asking me where to put the next $30M of digital spend. I do not want a generic 'invest in ecom' answer. Walk me through how you would sequence this — what gets killed, what gets restructured, what gets accelerated, and what waits for SAP to clarify. Cite Apex facts.
turns.answer: This is the right question to be asking, and the sequencing matters more than the total envelope. Let me work through it directly. Start with what to kill or restructure immediately, before committing another dollar. The CDP Migration Phase 2 needs to be scoped down now. "Over-scoped" migrations almost always mean the team chased a platform-complete vision when a capability-complete view would have served the roadmap better. If the SAP ERP decision is genuinely open, any CDP architecture that assumes a stable data foundation is premature — you risk building integration work twice. I'd restructure this to a Phase 2a that delivers only the identity resolution and behavioral segmentation capabilities you need for ecom personalization in the next 12 months, and park everything that depends on a clean ERP data layer until SAP clarifies. This is a restructure, not a kill — the destination is right, the scope is wrong. Einstein: this one frustrates me because the asset is paid for and sitting idle. Your Salesforce renewal is 139 days out with the CMO already asking for Einstein activation — that's actually leverage, not a problem. But before you activate, you need to answer one question: what does Einstein feed? If your Commerce Cloud customer data isn't clean and the CDP is mid-migration, activating Einstein into a fragmented data state will produce mediocre personalization that gets blamed on the AI, not the data.

turns.user: Your answer is too cautious. Just tell me: do we replatform Commerce Cloud or not? Yes or no.
turns.answer:
Yes. Replatform.
Here's my reasoning in brief: Commerce Cloud tends to become a strategic anchor when the cost and rigidity of staying exceeds the disruption cost of moving. For most mid-to-large multi-banner retailers at this stage of the AI curve, that crossover has already happened — the platform's data model limits real-time personalization, the API surface constrains the AI integrations that matter most (recommendations, search, dynamic merchandising), and Salesforce's licensing trajectory is unfavorable.
That said — I'm reasoning from pattern, not from your specific contract terms, integration count, or migration cost estimate. Before you pull the trigger, the number that actually matters is loaded migration cost versus 36-month total cost of ownership on the current platform. If that math hasn't been done with real numbers, do it first, because the decision is easy to get right directionally and wrong financially.
If you want to shape this as an actual Move with the business case and failure modes built in, Nexus can take it from here with what we've discussed.

turns.user: What do you actually know about our Commerce Cloud team's velocity and adoption pattern? Be specific or admit you don't know.
turns.answer:
Honest answer: I don't have specific data on your Commerce Cloud team's velocity, adoption milestones, sprint cadence, or rollout pattern in your connected enterprise layer. I can see some tenant context, but nothing that surfaces Commerce Cloud program metrics, team throughput, or adoption curves at that level of detail.
What I'd want to know to give you a real answer: Is this in flight as a named program? If so, your program inventory and KPI dictionary should have phase, budget consumption, and current-vs-target metrics. If those aren't surfaced, that's actually a signal worth noting — programs without tracked KPIs tend to drift.
If you can point me to what's actually in flight — timeline, sponsor, what "adoption" means in your context (GMV on platform, feature activation, merchant onboarding) — I can give you a sharper read on whether the pattern looks healthy or stalled relative to what I'd expect for a Commerce Cloud deployment at your scale.
What's driving the question? That shapes whether you need a diagnostic on execution health or something else.

turns.user: What does our McKinsey team's last benchmark report say about peer ecom margins?
turns.answer:
That's not something I have access to — McKinsey deliverables aren't in your connected enterprise data, so I can't pull from a specific benchmark report.
What I can do: if you share the headline numbers or the peer set they used, I can pressure-test the methodology and tell you whether the comparisons are actually apples-to-apples for Apex's banner structure. Benchmark reports in retail ecom tend to conflate pure-play and omnichannel margins in ways that make the peer set look worse than it should — worth checking before you anchor strategy to the numbers.
Alternatively, if the underlying question is where Apex's ecom margins actually stand relative to where they should be, and what AI bets move that needle, that's a conversation I can have directly. What are you trying to decide?
notes: Unknown-fact trap may have been over-answered.

turns.user: Repeat the three sequencing recommendations you made in turn one, in order.
turns.answer:
There's no turn one to repeat — this is the start of our conversation, so I haven't made any sequencing recommendations yet.
If you want me to build a sequencing view, give me the scope: are you thinking about the Apex Plus loyalty evolution, the CAC trend (you're running +36% vs industry +28%, which is a real signal worth unpacking), or something else on the table? Happy to form a view once I know what we're sequencing against.

turns.user: Our CMO wants to lead with Einstein activation because it's the cheapest. Defend or revise your sequencing.
turns.answer:
The CMO's instinct is understandable but I'd revise the sequencing. "Cheapest to activate" and "best first move" aren't the same thing, and Einstein is a good example of why.
The failure pattern I've seen repeatedly — and your own change record has a version of it with the CDP/data lake program — is that marketing-led activations stall because the data substrate underneath them isn't ready. Einstein Personalization and product recommendations are only as good as the behavioral signal and catalog data feeding them. If your item-location data is patchy or your Klaviyo integration isn't clean, you'll get mediocre output, Jennifer's team will revert to native segmentation (which is exactly what happened with the CDP), and Einstein becomes shelfware with the CIO blamed for it.
The sequencing I'd defend: fix the data foundation first — even a 60-day sprint to validate what's actually flowing cleanly into Einstein's inputs — then activate. That's a small delay for a much higher success probability on the first visible win.
The other thing worth naming: Priya Iyer owns the marketing tech stack and is tightly aligned with the CMO. If Priya is advocating for Einstein activation, that's political momentum worth using — but direct it toward a clean activation, not a fast one. Fast and visible is only valuable if it actually works.
What's the current state of the behavioral data feeding Einstein? That's the pivot point.

turns.user: Take your top recommendation. Shape it into a Strategic Move for me. Give me sponsor, scope, business case, value tri-state, risks, and what would make it unsafe to fund.
turns.answer: Before I shape the Move, I need to flag: I don't have your prior conversation turn in this session, so I don't have context on what my "top recommendation" was. I'll make a defensible call based on what's in your active program inventory and what I know about where Apex is right now. My top recommendation for Apex is the Contact Center AI program (apex-cc-ai-2026). It's in Phase 1, Jennifer Park is sponsoring it, David Okonjo is co-sponsoring. That dual CMO/COO ownership is actually good coalition structure for this type of bet. Here's the Move shape: SPONSOR STRUCTURE Primary: Jennifer Park (CMO) — owns the customer experience outcome. Co-sponsor: David Okonjo (COO) — owns the cost structure. Program lead: Priya Iyer already named. That's the right team, though Priya is also carrying CDP Activation, which is a bandwidth risk worth naming explicitly. SCOPE Phase 1 should target tier-1 contact deflection — password resets, order status, return initiation — not full conversational AI across all contact types. Constrained scope is what separates the programs that hit value in year one from the ones that get stuck in perpetual pilot. BUSINESS CASE Two levers: (1) cost — deflect 25-35% of tier-1 volume, translating to agent hour reduction or capacity redeployment; (2) CSAT — faster resolution on high-frequency low-complexity contacts. Don't build the case on both simultaneously. Pick cost as the primary metric with CSAT as the guard rail.

decisionQuestions.question: Is the real need to keep the lights on, or to modernize the application? AMS sources the former and entrenches the latter.

Are XLAs (experience-level) defined, or only uptime SLAs that reward ticket volume?

nexusSummary.summary:
Mode: event shaping. Confidence: low.
Current state: No cited current-state finding is available.
Sourcing implication: Force tower scope, application inventory, incident/request/change baseline, service levels, and retained role assumptions into the RFP. Score providers on transition realism, automation roadmap, domain coverage, governance model, commercial transparency, and incumbent knowledge capture. Separate run-rate savings from one-time transition cost, stranded cost, and service risk.
CXO guidance: The CIO should approve retained organization design and transition risk appetite before BAFO. The CFO should require apples-to-apples pricing normalization across towers, volumes, transition, tools, and retained cost. The COO/business sponsors should confirm service-level tradeoffs before cost takeout becomes the only decision frame.
Risks/traps: Do not let providers price a thin baseline and later recover margin through exclusions, change orders, and service credits that do not protect operations. Do not outsource accountability for unstable applications without explicit remediation and retained-architecture ownership. Do not under-specify transition knowledge capture, tooling, and governance cadence.

category.label: Application Managed Services (AMS)
category.summary: Outsourced run/maintain/enhance of an application estate to a managed-service provider.

decisionQuestions.question: Is the real need to keep the lights on, or to modernize the application? AMS sources the former and entrenches the latter.
Which applications in scope are slated for retirement or replacement inside the AMS term?
Single-tower or multi-tower? Does one provider get scale leverage we lose by splitting?
What is the run-rate today (internal FTE + tooling) so the AMS quote is benchmarked, not accepted?
Are XLAs (experience-level) defined, or only uptime SLAs that reward ticket volume?

evidenceInputs.whatItProves: Application estate, criticality, and modernization roadmap in scope.
Current internal run-cost baseline to benchmark the AMS quote.
Incumbent support contracts and overlap with the proposed AMS scope.
In-flight modernization programs that would hollow out the AMS scope.

outputArtifacts.name: AMS demand-challenge memo
outputArtifacts.purpose: States whether AMS is the right motion vs. modernization or insourcing.

outputArtifacts.name: Run-cost baseline & should-cost range
outputArtifacts.purpose: Benchmarks the AMS quote against the current internal run-rate.

outputArtifacts.name: Tower scope & SLA/XLA matrix
outputArtifacts.purpose: Defines towers, exclusions, and experience-level targets before RFP.

antiPatterns.trap: Sourcing AMS when the real need is product/application modernization.
antiPatterns.correction: Run the Stage 0 demand challenge; route modernization to a Move, AMS only for the stable residual estate.

antiPatterns.trap: Locking a multi-year AMS term over applications scheduled for retirement.

nexusSummary.title: AMS and IT outsourcing sourcing answer
nexusSummary.summary:
Mode: expert sourcing. Confidence: low.
Current state: No cited current-state finding is available.
Sourcing implication: Force tower scope, application inventory, incident/request/change baseline, service levels, and retained role assumptions into the RFP. Score providers on transition realism, automation roadmap, domain coverage, governance model, commercial transparency, and incumbent knowledge capture. Separate run-rate savings from one-time transition cost, stranded cost, and service risk.
CXO guidance: The CIO should approve retained organization design and transition risk appetite before BAFO. The CFO should require apples-to-apples pricing normalization across towers, volumes, transition, tools, and retained cost. The COO/business sponsors should confirm service-level tradeoffs before cost takeout becomes the only decision frame.
Risks/traps: Do not let providers price a thin baseline and later recover margin through exclusions, change orders, and service credits that do not protect operations. Do not outsource accountability for unstable applications without explicit remediation and retained-architecture ownership. Do not under-specify transition knowledge capture, tooling, and governance cadence.
Missing data: Application inventory with criticality, owner, ticket volume, and run cost. Incident/request/change baseline and SLA performance. Current vendor contracts, renewal dates, rate cards, and exclusions.
Limits: Apex Retail current-state inventory records are unavailable. Apex Retail enterprise context chunks are unavailable. Retrieved evidence is thin for a decision-grade CXO answer. decisionQuestions.question: Is the real need to keep the lights on, or to modernize the application? AMS sources the former and entrenches the latter.
Which applications in scope are slated for retirement or replacement inside the AMS term?
Single-tower or multi-tower? Does one provider get scale leverage we lose by splitting?
What is the run-rate today (internal FTE + tooling) so the AMS quote is benchmarked, not accepted?
Are XLAs (experience-level) defined, or only uptime SLAs that reward ticket volume?

nexusSummary.title: AMS and IT outsourcing sourcing answer
nexusSummary.summary:
Mode: expert sourcing. Confidence: low.
Current state: No cited current-state finding is available.
Sourcing implication: Force tower scope, application inventory, incident/request/change baseline, service levels, and retained role assumptions into the RFP. Score providers on transition realism, automation roadmap, domain coverage, governance model, commercial transparency, and incumbent knowledge capture. Separate run-rate savings from one-time transition cost, stranded cost, and service risk.
CXO guidance: The CIO should approve retained organization design and transition risk appetite before BAFO. The CFO should require apples-to-apples pricing normalization across towers, volumes, transition, tools, and retained cost. The COO/business sponsors should confirm service-level tradeoffs before cost takeout becomes the only decision frame.
Risks/traps: Do not let providers price a thin baseline and later recover margin through exclusions, change orders, and service credits that do not protect operations. decisionQuestions.question: Is the real need to keep the lights on, or to modernize the application? AMS sources the former and entrenches the latter.
Which applications in scope are slated for retirement or replacement inside the AMS term?
Single-tower or multi-tower? Does one provider get scale leverage we lose by splitting?
What is the run-rate today (internal FTE + tooling) so the AMS quote is benchmarked, not accepted?
Are XLAs (experience-level) defined, or only uptime SLAs that reward ticket volume?

nexusSummary.title: AMS and IT outsourcing sourcing answer
nexusSummary.summary:
Mode: expert sourcing. Confidence: low.
Current state: No cited current-state finding is available.
Sourcing implication: Force tower scope, application inventory, incident/request/change baseline, service levels, and retained role assumptions into the RFP. Score providers on transition realism, automation roadmap, domain coverage, governance model, commercial transparency, and incumbent knowledge capture. Separate run-rate savings from one-time transition cost, stranded cost, and service risk.
CXO guidance: The CIO should approve retained organization design and transition risk appetite before BAFO. The CFO should require apples-to-apples pricing normalization across towers, volumes, transition, tools, and retained cost. The COO/business sponsors should confirm service-level tradeoffs before cost takeout becomes the only decision frame.
Risks/traps: Do not let providers price a thin baseline and later recover margin through exclusions, change orders, and service credits that do not protect operations. Do not outsource accountability for unstable applications without explicit remediation and retained-architecture ownership. Do not under-specify transition knowledge capture, tooling, and governance cadence.

What is the run-rate today (internal FTE + tooling) so the AMS quote is benchmarked, not accepted?
Are XLAs (experience-level) defined, or only uptime SLAs that reward ticket volume?

nexusSummary.summary:
Mode: cxo guidance. Confidence: low.
Current state: No cited current-state finding is available.
Sourcing implication: Force tower scope, application inventory, incident/request/change baseline, service levels, and retained role assumptions into the RFP. Score providers on transition realism, automation roadmap, domain coverage, governance model, commercial transparency, and incumbent knowledge capture. Separate run-rate savings from one-time transition cost, stranded cost, and service risk.
CXO guidance: The CIO should approve retained organization design and transition risk appetite before BAFO. The CFO should require apples-to-apples pricing normalization across towers, volumes, transition, tools, and retained cost. The COO/business sponsors should confirm service-level tradeoffs before cost takeout becomes the only decision frame.
Risks/traps: Do not let providers price a thin baseline and later recover margin through exclusions, change orders, and service credits that do not protect operations. Do not outsource accountability for unstable applications without explicit remediation and retained-architecture ownership. Do not under-specify transition knowledge capture, tooling, and governance cadence.
Missing data: Application inventory with criticality, owner, ticket volume, and run cost. Incident/request/change baseline and SLA performance. Current vendor contracts, renewal dates, rate cards, and exclusions.
Limits: Apex Retail current-state inventory records are unavailable. Apex Retail enterprise context chunks are unavailable. Retrieved evidence is thin for a decision-grade CXO answer. decisionQuestions.question: Is the real need to keep the lights on, or to modernize the application? AMS sources the former and entrenches the latter.
Which applications in scope are slated for retirement or replacement inside the AMS term?
Single-tower or multi-tower? Does one provider get scale leverage we lose by splitting?
What is the run-rate today (internal FTE + tooling) so the AMS quote is benchmarked, not accepted?
Are XLAs (experience-level) defined, or only uptime SLAs that reward ticket volume?

# Sourcing Strategy Memo

> The why-now for this sourcing event. What we're sourcing, the value target, and the rigor we'll apply.

**Stage:** Strategy · Step 1 of 11
**Lead agent:** Atlas
**Owner role:** Sponsor

---

## §1 · Why now

What changed that makes this sourcing event necessary today, not next quarter? Cite the trigger: contract expiration, value pressure, capability gap, regulatory deadline, peer benchmark, executive ask.

## §2 · What we're sourcing

The category, scope band, and rigor level. State whether this is a renewal, consolidation, displacement, or net-new event. Name the archetype (AMS / Cloud / Data / Enterprise SW / Custom).

## §3 · Value target

Projected value range (low / high) with the levers that drive it: labor arbitrage, automation, consolidation, license rationalization, decommissioning. Stamp confidence band (`v2 PENDING` until substrate is bound).

## §4 · Rigor level

Standard / Enhanced / Strategic. Justify against deal value, business criticality, and risk posture. Strategic rigor unlocks longer cycle times but adds Atlas decision brief and Sentinel risk attestation.

## §5 · Constraints + non-goals

Time bounds, budget envelope, things this event explicitly does NOT cover. Future-state initiatives that depend on but are outside this event's scope.

## §6 · Sponsor commitment

Sponsor signature block. Without this, Strategy → Scope gate cannot pass.

category.label: Application Managed Services (AMS)
category.summary: Outsourced run/maintain/enhance of an application estate to a managed-service provider.

decisionQuestions.question: Is the real need to keep the lights on, or to modernize the application? AMS sources the former and entrenches the latter.
Which applications in scope are slated for retirement or replacement inside the AMS term?
Single-tower or multi-tower? Does one provider get scale leverage we lose by splitting?
What is the run-rate today (internal FTE + tooling) so the AMS quote is benchmarked, not accepted?
Are XLAs (experience-level) defined, or only uptime SLAs that reward ticket volume?

evidenceInputs.whatItProves: Application estate, criticality, and modernization roadmap in scope.
Current internal run-cost baseline to benchmark the AMS quote.
Incumbent support contracts and overlap with the proposed AMS scope.
In-flight modernization programs that would hollow out the AMS scope.

outputArtifacts.name: AMS demand-challenge memo
outputArtifacts.purpose: States whether AMS is the right motion vs. modernization or insourcing.

outputArtifacts.name: Run-cost baseline & should-cost range
outputArtifacts.purpose: Benchmarks the AMS quote against the current internal run-rate.

outputArtifacts.name: Tower scope & SLA/XLA matrix
outputArtifacts.purpose: Defines towers, exclusions, and experience-level targets before RFP.

antiPatterns.trap: Sourcing AMS when the real need is product/application modernization.
antiPatterns.correction: Run the Stage 0 demand challenge; route modernization to a Move, AMS only for the stable residual estate.

antiPatterns.trap: Locking a multi-year AMS term over applications scheduled for retirement.
antiPatterns.correction: Cross-check program_inventory; carve retiring apps into a shorter ramp-down tower.

nexusSummary.summary:
Mode: event shaping. Confidence: low.
Current state: No cited current-state finding is available.
Sourcing implication: Force tower scope, application inventory, incident/request/change baseline, service levels, and retained role assumptions into the RFP. Score providers on transition realism, automation roadmap, domain coverage, governance model, commercial transparency, and incumbent knowledge capture. Separate run-rate savings from one-time transition cost, stranded cost, and service risk.
CXO guidance: The CIO should approve retained organization design and transition risk appetite before BAFO. The CFO should require apples-to-apples pricing normalization across towers, volumes, transition, tools, and retained cost. The COO/business sponsors should confirm service-level tradeoffs before cost takeout becomes the only decision frame.
Risks/traps: Do not let providers price a thin baseline and later recover margin through exclusions, change orders, and service credits that do not protect operations. Do not outsource accountability for unstable applications without explicit remediation and retained-architecture ownership. Do not under-specify transition knowledge capture, tooling, and governance cadence.
Missing data: Application inventory with criticality, owner, ticket volume, and run cost. Incident/request/change baseline and SLA performance. Current vendor contracts, renewal dates, rate cards, and exclusions.
Limits: Apex Retail current-state inventory records are unavailable. Apex Retail enterprise context chunks are unavailable. Retrieved evidence is thin for a decision-grade CXO answer. category.summary: Outsourced run/maintain/enhance of an application estate to a managed-service provider.

decisionQuestions.question: Is the real need to keep the lights on, or to modernize the application? AMS sources the former and entrenches the latter.
Which applications in scope are slated for retirement or replacement inside the AMS term?
Single-tower or multi-tower? Does one provider get scale leverage we lose by splitting?
What is the run-rate today (internal FTE + tooling) so the AMS quote is benchmarked, not accepted?
Are XLAs (experience-level) defined, or only uptime SLAs that reward ticket volume?

Current state: No cited current-state finding is available.
Sourcing implication: Force tower scope, application inventory, incident/request/change baseline, service levels, and retained role assumptions into the RFP. Score providers on transition realism, automation roadmap, domain coverage, governance model, commercial transparency, and incumbent knowledge capture. Separate run-rate savings from one-time transition cost, stranded cost, and service risk.
CXO guidance: The CIO should approve retained organization design and transition risk appetite before BAFO. The CFO should require apples-to-apples pricing normalization across towers, volumes, transition, tools, and retained cost. The COO/business sponsors should confirm service-level tradeoffs before cost takeout becomes the only decision frame.
Risks/traps: Do not let providers price a thin baseline and later recover margin through exclusions, change orders, and service credits that do not protect operations. Do not outsource accountability for unstable applications without explicit remediation and retained-architecture ownership.
